explanations.explanation: Wail is the word, friend. Isaiah opens with “Wail, O ships of Tarshish…” (Isaiah 23:1). Tarshish is a faraway port, and the news is so heavy that even the ships get told to cry out. I think that's about the saddest way you could start a message.

Rejoice would be a party, and this message is no party. Isaiah says “Wail, O ships of Tarshish…” because Tyre is laid waste. I understand grabbing the cheerful one, friend, because I'd reach for the confetti too. But this burden opens with crying, not cheering.

Anchor sounds sensible for a ship, I'll give you that. But Isaiah doesn't tell the ships to park. He tells them to wail, because Tyre is laid waste. When even the ships are told to cry, you know the news is serious.

explanations.answer: Tyre is laid waste with no house or harbor
explanations.explanation: That's the reason Isaiah gives. Tyre is laid waste, “without house or harbor.” Ships sail toward a port, so I think a city with no harbor left is news that hits them hard. That's a lot of loss packed into one verse.

explanations.answer: Tyre has closed its harbor to their ships
explanations.explanation: This one sounds like a locked front door, but that's not what Isaiah says. Nobody shut anything on the ships. Tyre is laid waste, and there is no harbor left at all. A closed door can be opened again, friend, but that's not the picture here.

explanations.answer: Tyre has gone to war against Tarshish
explanations.explanation: Isaiah never says Tyre fights Tarshish. Tyre is the one who is laid waste. The ships of Tarshish are called to wail over her, not to brace for a fight. I think that makes them mourners here, not enemies.
True, friend. The verse says word has reached them from the land of Cyprus. So the news about Tyre arrives from across the water. The ships hear it before they ever see it.

This one is true, friend. Isaiah says, “Word has reached them from the land of Cyprus.” The news about Tyre comes to the ships of Tarshish from Cyprus. It's an easy detail to slide past, so no shame in that.

True. Isaiah says, “Be silent, O dwellers of the coastland, you merchants of Sidon…” (Isaiah 23:2). These are traders who spent their days making deals and crossing the sea. Now they're told to hush. I'd bet that's the quietest that coast ever got.

It's actually true, friend. Isaiah tells the dwellers of the coastland, the merchants of Sidon, “Be silent…” (Isaiah 23:2). These are people whose traders had crossed the sea. Now the message to them is to go quiet.

Merchant is right. Isaiah says Tyre “was the merchant of the nations” (Isaiah 23:3). Grain from the Nile came across the water, and its harvest was Tyre's revenue. When the whole world's goods come through your harbor, that title fits.

Servant is a fair guess, but it's not the word Isaiah uses. Look at the picture, friend: ships haul in the Nile's harvest, and that harvest is Tyre's revenue. That's a trader's life, not a servant's. Isaiah calls her the merchant of the nations.

A shepherd keeps sheep, and nobody here is out in a pasture. Isaiah has ships crossing the great waters with the harvest of the Nile. That makes Tyre the merchant of the nations. I think you were picturing a very different postcard.

Ashamed is the word. Isaiah says, “Be ashamed, O Sidon, the stronghold of the sea…” (Isaiah 23:4). A stronghold is supposed to be a place that holds up. Tyre has been laid waste, and Sidon gets this message right after.
Glad would be a much happier verse, friend. But Isaiah tells Sidon to “Be ashamed…” and Sidon is called the stronghold of the sea. No cheering here. This message to Sidon comes as Tyre lies in ruins.
Brave sounds like a good pep talk for a stronghold. It's not what Isaiah says, though. He tells Sidon, “Be ashamed…” (Isaiah 23:4). Not a pep talk, friend, so no cheering section here.

That's what Isaiah says. “When the report reaches Egypt, they will writhe in agony over the news of Tyre” (Isaiah 23:5). Egypt's Nile harvest had flowed to Tyre, so this news lands close to home. I think that's why the word is so strong.

explanations.answer: They will cheer in the streets
explanations.explanation: No parade here, friend. Isaiah says that when the report reaches Egypt, they will writhe in agony. Egypt is the land whose harvest came to Tyre across the water. That's not cheering weather.

explanations.answer: They will send ships to help
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a kind neighbor, but Isaiah doesn't say it. He says Egypt will writhe in agony over the news of Tyre. The verse gives their reaction and nothing about any rescue fleet. I'd love a happier ending too, baker.

It's the other way around, friend. Isaiah calls Tyre a city “whose origin is from antiquity” (Isaiah 23:7). That means she's ancient, not brand new. This city has been around longer than anybody's grandmother's recipe.
False is right. Isaiah says Tyre's “origin is from antiquity” (Isaiah 23:7). She's an ancient city, and her feet have taken her to settle far away. Old city, long reach.
That's what Isaiah says. “The LORD of Hosts planned it…” (Isaiah 23:9). Isaiah asks who planned it, and then he answers his own question. Plain and direct, friend.

Egypt shows up in this passage, but Isaiah never names a pharaoh as the planner. Egypt is the one that will writhe in agony over the news. The verse answers the question outright: the LORD of Hosts planned it. Nice try, friend.

The merchants of Sidon are in the passage, but they aren't the planners. Isaiah tells them to be silent (Isaiah 23:2). When he asks who planned this, his own answer is “The LORD of Hosts planned it…” (Isaiah 23:9). They're hearing the news, not making it.

explanations.answer: To disgrace all the renowned of the earth
explanations.explanation: That's the reason Isaiah gives. The LORD of Hosts planned it “…to disgrace all the renowned of the earth.” The verse also says it was to defile all of Tyre's glorious beauty. Tyre had a famous name, and the verse goes straight at it.

explanations.answer: To hand its harbor over to Sidon
explanations.explanation: Sidon doesn't come out ahead in this passage. Isaiah tells Sidon to be ashamed (Isaiah 23:4). The reason the verse gives is “…to disgrace all the renowned of the earth.” Nobody gets a free harbor, friend.

explanations.answer: To repay it for a broken treaty
explanations.explanation: Isaiah never mentions a treaty here. The verse says the LORD of Hosts planned it to defile all of Tyre's glorious beauty and “…to disgrace all the renowned of the earth.” I'd stick with what the text says. Adding reasons it doesn't give is a trap, friend.

explanations.answer: There is no longer a harbor
explanations.explanation: Right, and the verse says it plainly: “there is no longer a harbor” (Isaiah 23:10). So the Daughter of Tarshish is told to work her land like the Nile. A ship town with no harbor needs a new plan. That's a big change of job, friend.
Isaiah says nothing about rain. The reason he gives is “there is no longer a harbor.” Without a harbor, the Daughter of Tarshish is told to cultivate her land. The weather report will have to wait.

explanations.answer: Egypt wants to buy her crops
explanations.explanation: Egypt is mentioned in the verse as a comparison, since the land is to be worked like the Nile. But Isaiah never says Egypt wants to buy anything. The stated reason is “there is no longer a harbor.” Don't go adding customers, friend.

Destroyed is right. The LORD “has given a command that the strongholds of Canaan be destroyed” (Isaiah 23:11). That's a big verse, because His hand is stretched out over the sea and kingdoms tremble. Heavy words, friend.

Spared would be a softer verse, friend. But the command is that the strongholds of Canaan be destroyed. This comes right after the LORD stretches out His hand over the sea and makes kingdoms tremble. This one is a hard word.
Guarded sounds like a safe ending for a stronghold. It's not the word in the verse. The LORD gave a command that the strongholds of Canaan be destroyed. Nobody's posting a night watch on these walls.

That's what the LORD says: “…even there you will find no rest.” Cyprus looks like the next stop on the map. But the Virgin Daughter of Sidon is told there is no rest there either. I think that's one of the hardest lines in the chapter.

Cyprus sounds like a safe island, I get it. But the LORD tells her, “…even there you will find no rest.” Safety isn't what the verse promises. She's told to go, and the verse says she'll find no rest.

Trading is a Tyre and Sidon kind of idea, so it's a natural guess. But the LORD doesn't mention trade here. He says, “…even there you will find no rest.” That's all the verse says about what waits in Cyprus.

True. Isaiah says of the land of the Chaldeans that “The Assyrians destined it for the desert creatures…” (Isaiah 23:13). They set up their siege towers, stripped its palaces and brought it to ruin. Isaiah points at that land as something to look at.

It's true, friend. Isaiah says the Assyrians set up their siege towers, stripped the palaces and “…brought it to ruin.” That's the land of the Chaldeans he's pointing to. The Assyrians are named right there in the verse.

Seventy is right. “At that time Tyre will be forgotten for seventy years—the span of a king's life” (Isaiah 23:15). Isaiah ties the number to a king's life. That's a long stretch to be forgotten, friend.
Seven is close in spelling, but it's not the number Isaiah gives. The verse says seventy years, the span of a king's life. That's ten times what you picked, friend. It's a very long wait.

Three years would be a quick nap compared to this. Isaiah says Tyre will be forgotten for seventy years, the span of a king's life. That's a whole lifetime of silence. Three isn't even in the neighborhood, baker.

That's the reason in the song. “Make sweet melody, sing many a song, so you will be remembered.” She's called a forgotten harlot, so the harp and the songs are meant to bring her back to people's minds. That's all the song gives as the reason.

explanations.answer: So she can leave the city
explanations.explanation: The song has her stroll through the city, not leave it. She takes up her harp and sings many a song for a reason, and the reason is “…so you will be remembered.” Nobody's packing a bag in this verse, friend.

explanations.answer: So the king will pardon her
explanations.explanation: Pardon is a nice idea, but no king or pardon shows up in the song. The reason it gives is “…so you will be remembered.” She's forgotten, and the music is meant to change that. Let's stay with what's on the page.
The ending goes the other way, friend. Isaiah says, “And at the end of seventy years, the LORD will restore Tyre.” The forgetting has an end date. Tyre doesn't stay forgotten for good.
False is right. Isaiah says, “…at the end of seventy years, the LORD will restore Tyre” (Isaiah 23:17). The seventy years of being forgotten come to an end. That's the turn in the verse.
It's the opposite, friend. Isaiah says Tyre's profits and wages “…will not be stored or saved…” (Isaiah 23:18). No vault, no stash, no rainy day jar. That's quite a switch for a city of merchants.

False is right. Isaiah says her profits and wages will be set apart to the LORD, and they “will not be stored or saved.” Tyre was a city that lived on revenue, so this is a big change. The money has a different destination.

That's what the verse says. Her profit goes to those who live before the LORD, “…for abundant food and fine clothing.” That's the last verse of the chapter, and it lands somewhere nobody would've guessed. Plenty to eat and good things to wear, friend.

Walls and towers fit a stronghold, and Canaan's strongholds were just mentioned. But that's not what this profit buys. Isaiah says it's for “…abundant food and fine clothing.” Think pantry and closet, not fortress.

explanations.answer: New ships and a safe harbor
explanations.explanation: Ships and a harbor are all over this chapter, so that's a very natural guess. But the verse says the profit goes to those who live before the LORD “…for abundant food and fine clothing.” Nothing in it mentions ships. This time the money goes to people, friend.
